418.t: Disc jockeys playing one thing over and over
418.s: He says radio programmers plug one kind of music and should give variety, which benefits advertisers too.
418.ch: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
418.q: I think somebody should get on them and tell them to change their tactics. Because they would get more listening for their...especially for their channel...now what is it...stations... Their station will have more listening. It's better for the people that are advertising, the things they're…

418.t: Variety in radio: country, rock and roll and the rest
418.s: Country and rock are fine but he objects to hearing one type constantly and wishes radio gave variety.
418.ch: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
418.q: And don't play too much of any type, but give everybody a chance to hear something. Some people like to hear pretty music, beautiful music, you know. I can stand listening to any type of music played once, one piece, one thing. But if you're going to keep cramming it down my throat, every number I…

510.t: The state of jazz radio and smooth jazz
510.s: Alias and Rowe lament that jazz radio plays smooth jazz and audiences do not know Coltrane; he contrasts it with the London band.
510.ch: Own bands and the England tour
510.q: I mean you can see the course of the way the music is going. You turn on what supposedly is a jazz station and they’re not really playing contemporary improvisatory jazz. Improvisatory is a big word for me, because that’s music that’s coming off of the top of your head. And the way the music is…

682.t: Small speakers and the car radio mix
682.s: Hank scorns producers who want a cassette mix to check in their cars and says mixes should be made for the best speakers.
682.q: Car radios was always the answer. I worked with producers, “Give me a mix, you put it on a cassette, I’m going to play it in my car.” That’s nuts. Is his car now the epitome of this is what it’s going to sound like? No. You’re going to make a sound for the best speakers you can. That will always…

958.t: Radio play, the Internet and file trading
958.s: The band falls between straight-ahead jazz and smooth jazz formats, getting only occasional public radio play. Fleck sees free trading as a problem and expects home recording to matter more than major labels.
958.q: Yeah. Like for instance if you’ve got a straight ahead jazz show we’re too something, we’re not a straight ahead jazz group. And if you have a contemporary jazz show that tends to be smooth jazz, we’re not smooth jazz so that knocks us out of jazz play unless you just have college or more…

105.t: Jazz radio stations never play his music
105.s: Stations play little real jazz and turn young people away.
105.q: It’s like how can you duplicate Trane? How can you duplicate Bird or Sweets or Prez or Diz? You know it’s just like these so-called radio stations. They call themselves jazz stations. Now I purposely don’t listen to them, but I listened to them all last week, right? Because I was home. And the…

593.s: Clear Channel dominates radio while Americana networks keep roots music alive.
593.q: There used to be these free-form FM stations. Some of them still may exist. Well there is a network sort of, although it’s not a formal network, of Americana or Roots music, and that’s where some of these good country players can still get an audience. But in terms of hearing them in a big city or…

334.t: Jazz on Japanese radio and young listeners
334.s: Few stations play jazz; young people hear loud rock and he listens to classical.
334.q: Can I say — loud. Loud music. And many radio stations [grunts] just like this. Just like rock music.

416.t: Radio, television and why TV hurt jazz
416.s: Radio was everything then; he argues television favored performers who moved and used lights.
416.q: Radio was the only thing then. There was no television you know. Every town you went to they played them, you’d make interviews, and it was, radio was the whole thing. Not like today. Television knocked us out of the box.

739.t: Radio programming integrity and record promoters
739.s: Poston tells his hosts not to play music they dislike despite pressure from radio promotion people.
739.q: Yeah. The way we handle it, and this is on me because I’m the one who has said this is how we’re going to handle it, our music director gets — I can’t even begin to tell you how many CDs we still get a day.

991.t: Dizzy on improvising as painting; jazz is not elevator music
991.s: Rowe quotes Mike Longo on Dizzy and rhythm; Sandoval says improvising is like a speech and that jazz needs attentive listening and more radio support.
991.ch: Career, recognition and jazz in America
991.q: He also said, “Improvising is like painting on the canvas” you know. You mix the color, you create shades and this and that. It’s like you’re creating — you have to imagine the whole picture in your mind when you are improvising. It’s like creating a speech for something. A good speech in America…

447.t: Jazz on the radio, smooth jazz and WUCF
447.s: More jazz on public radio; he rejects smooth jazz as lacking swing and praises Orlando station WUCF.
447.q: Yes, constantly. And I will say that there seems to be more jazz on the radio now than there was say ten years ago. But most of the stations are public radio stations or college stations and so forth. In Orlando we have WUCF which is an excellent jazz station. Now it depends on what you’re talking…

412.s: Hodes says the enemy is ignorance. DeMichael blames record companies and Hodes complains of the radio desert.
412.q: In everything. If people were hip to what jazz was, jazz wouldn't be struggling. The kids would get to hear it. Why isn't it that a kid cannot turn on his radio and

170.t: Rock and roll, the jukebox and radio
170.s: Musicians flee rock jukeboxes and radio is mostly rock or fusion.
170.q: Well, let me tell you about that now. There are clubs -- just like Slugs -- they playing all that -- you know, when it was open -- playing all that good music in there -- Lee Morgan Marvin, that's where he died at -- playing and when he'd get off the stand, they'd turn on the jukebox and they got…

529.t: The layman, the back beat and a freedom radio program
529.s: The working listener just wants the beat; Sam switches off a WBGO announcer who plays only freedom music.
529.ch: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
529.q: See he parked his finger in there because that back beat is there and he could pop his finger and he'd pat his feet and he could get up and shake his butt man and do anything he wanted to do because that beat is not going anywhere, you see. And all of that conversation while we was talking lead us…

98.t: Nostalgia craze and his call-in jazz radio shows
98.s: Saunders sees a nostalgic return to older players and recalls radio appearances on jazz stations where listeners called in.
98.ch: Changing styles, the road and nightlife
98.q: I don't know. People -- you can't hardly predict what people will do. But one of the fortunate things that has happened in the last few years is the nostalgic craze. Everybody's going back, and then you find these guys, they're digging them up out of the woodwork, and these guys are coming back and…
